Pele Yoetz 359:3: And there are transgressions a person does not know at all are transgressions, and some are counted in his eyes as a commandment, in the manner of what is written (Proverbs 14:12), “There is a way that seems straight to a man, but its end is the ways of death.” And like the servant of Rabbi Akiva at the beginning of his service, as told in the Talmud (Derech Eretz Zuta, ch. 8), who found a corpse requiring burial and carried it on his shoulder and brought it to the city, and our sages, of blessed memory, said to him, “For every step you took, you became liable for death at the hand of the Omnipresent.” Then he said, “If this is so when I thought I was performing a commandment, how much more so when I think of committing a transgression” — he immediately accepted upon himself to engage in Torah.
Pele Yoetz 359:4: And great is the evil of the common person, who walks in darkness, forbidding what is permitted and permitting what is forbidden, going from evil to evil, and God shall bring everyone into judgment, for an unwitting error of not having studied is elevated to willfulness (Avot 4:13; Bava Metzia 33b). And it is written (Jeremiah 9:11), “For what did the land perish? Because they abandoned My Torah.” And it is written (Proverbs 28:9), “Whoever turns his ear away from hearing the Torah, even his prayer is an abomination.” For sometimes he thinks he is performing a commandment and presses himself and prays while drunk, or while needing to relieve himself, so as not to let the time for prayer pass, yet his prayer is an abomination. And likewise in this manner, one who does not study and does not hear teachings has no moment without mishap and no step without transgression. And it is likewise written in Sefer Chasidim (sec. 153) that a person is judged and punished for what he did not know, because he did not take it to heart to know, for it is written (Numbers 22:34), “I have sinned, for I did not know that you stood against me” — meaning, “I have sinned in that I did not take it to heart to know and understand.”
Pele Yoetz 359:5: Behold, therefore, let a man gather strength and overcome his inclination and run to the study house to hear teachings, even against his will, not for his own pleasure, and nullify his own will before the Creator's will, and in the end it shall be pleasant and sweet to him. And let him take to heart the reward of the commandment, for the reward of going is in his hand, and the reward of hearing, and the reward of answering “Yehei shmei rabba,” and that they tear up his decree and forgive him all his sins, and out of doing it not for its own sake he comes to do it for its own sake, for he shall understand how much satisfaction he gives his Creator, since He pays such good reward — and there is no reward in the world as great as a person meriting, mere breath that he is, to give satisfaction to his Creator.
Pele Yoetz 359:6: And this is a great principle in the Torah: that one should reckon the reward of a commandment even as though it were worth a thousand gold coins, and just as one strives, toils, and labors to earn a thousand gold coins, so should he strive and labor to fulfill every good thing, and believe with complete faith in what is true and firmly established without any doubt whatsoever, that no amount of silver, gold, and jewels in the world could match the value of even the smallest commandment, and that the good of the World to Come is beyond comparison and beyond the grasp of our own hands while we are still creatures of matter, to the point that our sages, of blessed memory, said (Avot 4:17): one hour of tranquility of spirit in the World to Come is better than all the life of this world, even if one were to live the life of a king. Go and learn from the wicked Nebuchadnezzar, whom the Holy One, blessed be He, wished to repay in this world for the reward of the four steps he took for the honor of the Omnipresent, and gave him a kingdom and dominion such that he ruled with his own hand and had power even over the beasts of the field, riding on the lion and tying the serpent as a bridle around its neck (Sanhedrin 96a) — how much more so should our reward for the World to Come be exceedingly great, since even the emptiest among us are as full of commandments as a pomegranate. But a person should not say, “If so, I have more than enough for the World to Come,” for the World to Come is a world whose understanding is vast, and the reward is such an important matter that one must do much in order to merit even one hour of tranquility of spirit for the World to Come. In any case, let him know with certainty that for every good deed he performs, whether in thought, speech, or deed, he certainly gains reward far greater than thousands of gold and silver, and regarding this it is said (Proverbs 2:4-5), “If you seek it as silver and search for it as for hidden treasures, then you shall understand the fear of the Lord.” Behold, therefore, to every place where there is a study session, let him run like a deer to hear teachings, for there is no study session without some novel insight. And come and see how much effort and running is required for words of Torah, for it is written (Deuteronomy 30:12), “It is not in heaven, nor is it beyond the sea.” And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Eruvin 55a) that had it been in heaven or beyond the sea, you would have needed to go after it, and how much more so now that it is in the land and within the city, that one should not fail to go after it, and even if he does not learn any novel insight, the reward for going, the reward for hearing, and the reward for answering “Yehei shmei rabba” are in his hand.
Pele Yoetz 359:7: And when he goes to the study house, let his ears be attentive to the words of the sermon with great affection, and when he hears something new, let him write it on the tablet of his heart, and let it be a reminder before his eyes to observe, do, and fulfill, for this is the entire fruit of hearing — not like many of the common people who, even when they force themselves and go to the study house, have ears yet do not hear, to the point that if you were to ask them immediately what novel insight was taught at the study house, they would not know. And there are those who give heart to listen, and when they hear several matters they have stumbled in, their flesh pains them and they grieve, but afterward it is forgotten from their heart and the world continues as its custom, and they add transgression to their sin, for what was until now unwitting is now deliberate. And the early ones already explained the statement of King David, peace be upon him, who said (Psalms 34:12), “Come, children, listen to me; I shall teach you the fear of the Lord.” He did not say, “Come, children, listen to me,” meaning: I know that while you are at the study house you will listen to me, but the essential thing depends on your carrying the words engraved in your hearts after you leave and heeding me to observe and act. And if they said that the segulah of hearing the sermon is to restrain transgression and remove sin, this is certainly when doing it properly, with ears attentive with great affection to the words of the living God, for his mouth speaks them. And as they explained in the Masorah that there are three instances of “venishma” [“and it was heard”] (Exodus 28:35), “and its sound shall be heard when he enters the sanctuary” referring to the wise man who expounds, one must make “we shall do and we shall hear” (Exodus 19:8), thinking that it is not he who speaks, but rather “and the king's decree shall be heard” (Esther 1:20), the decree of the King of the world, and he must be exceedingly careful to do all that he hears, and answer “Amen, yehei shmei rabba” with all his strength and all his intention — then it is accepted to atone for him.
Pele Yoetz 359:8: And just as it is a commandment to hear the words of the wise, who teach a person to know the statutes of God and His teachings and which is the straight way to walk in, and the deeds to do and the deeds not to do, correspondingly our sages, of blessed memory, said (Ketubot 5b): a person should not let his ear hear idle words, for the ears are burned first among the limbs. And they further said (ibid.): why do the fingers resemble stakes? And why is the entire ear hard while the earlobe is soft? So that if he hears something improper, he can bend the lobe into it and place his finger upon it so as not to hear, for hearing it is not good. And there are people who take great delight in hearing novelties, and there are those who, if they see two people talking and do not hear what they are saying, or heard half a matter and did not hear all of it, their soul departs and they writhe with great agitation, striving with all their might to know the matter, not resting or settling until they know it. And this is a bad illness called in our language “curiosity” [curiosite/neugierig], and it is vanity and vexation of spirit, for if there is a need to know the matter, let him seek it from its proper source to inform him, and if there is no need to know it, what does it give him and what does it add to know idle matters? And whoever has this bad trait does much evil: first, that he abandons the Torah, the source of living waters, to dig broken cisterns to hear novel matters, and these shall be his undoing, confusing his mind during his prayer, for all the novelties he heard gather together and come to him in his mind at the time of his prayer. And since he is eager to hear novel matters at every command, he lets himself become entangled and hears all kinds of forbidden speech, and if he remains silent and does not protest, he shall be punished as an accomplice; and since his soul desires to know novelties, he comes to dig to know another's secret and listen under the window and behind the wall, transgressing “you shall not go about as a talebearer among your people” (Leviticus 19:16), as I have written above under the entry Sod, in the name of Halachot Ketanot (part 1, sec. 276) — see there — in such a way that this bad trait of hearing novel matters did not go out to teach only about itself, but its companions are brought after it, going from evil to evil. Therefore it is good for a man not to heed the voice of whisperers, but rather those who murmur words of Torah, and let such matters be remembered and performed, and through this he shall merit the World to Come, to sit in the assembly of the holy.
Pele Yoetz 360:1: Sak (Sackcloth) — The matter of wearing sackcloth on one's flesh is good and exceedingly beneficial to restrain transgression and remove sin and for the acceptance of prayers, and its secret is exalted and lofty — see the holy book Reshit Chokhmah. Behold, therefore, whoever has as his entire aim to rectify his soul and give satisfaction to his Creator should make and prepare for himself a small garment of this kind to wear beneath his clothes at the time of reciting Tikkun Chatzot and when pouring out his speech, seeking forgiveness. And let him not be lazy about taking it off and putting it back on, and let him not be concerned about the cold in the winter months, for all this is as nothing compared to the benefit and compared to the love of the blessed Creator.
Pele Yoetz 360:2: And likewise, in this manner, whoever truly loves the Name should do every good and beneficial thing for atonement, such as rolling himself in snow and enduring lashes and self-mortification and every kind of suffering he can bear — all this is as nothing before them, and everything shall be light when weighed against the benefit and against the love of the Creator, for love is as fierce as death, and if its beginning is painful, after he does it, his heart shall rejoice and his glory shall exult that he has acted and given satisfaction to his Creator, and when he becomes accustomed, the habit becomes second nature for him to perform that good trait, and even when he grows old he shall not depart from it (Proverbs 22:6). And let the living take to heart that man is born to toil, and happy is he whose toil is in Torah and Divine service and gives satisfaction to his Creator — how good is his portion.
Pele Yoetz 361:1: Shevach (Praise) — Our sages, of blessed memory, said (Eruvin 18b): they mention part of a person's praise to his face, and all of it not to his face. And the reason it is not all said to his face appears to be so that his mind not become haughty and his heart not be lifted up. But part of it is said, so that he be diligent in doing good upon seeing that his deeds shall be praised in the gates, and also to increase love and brotherhood, peace and friendship, in such a way that a scale and balances of justice are needed: if one sees that a person is not so devoted to love of the Name, and there is concern that the service of the commandment shall be burdensome upon him, it is fitting to tell him the praise and reward of the commandment he performs, and say to him, “Happy are you, how good is your portion, that you acquire the World to Come through your deeds,” and similar things that kindle the heart, so that he hold fast to his strength to perform commandments, or so that they praise him, or in order to merit good reward, and out of not doing it for its own sake he comes to do it for its own sake. But for a good man who is devoted to love of the Name and does his deeds for the sake of Heaven, not so that they praise him, it is fitting to be careful and guard against praising him to his face at all, especially in this orphaned generation, for the inclination toward pride is a great evil, for our sages, of blessed memory, said (Sotah 5a): whoever has it is under a ban. Is it a small thing, what is written (Proverbs 16:5), “An abomination to the Lord is every haughty heart” — any degree of haughtiness of heart? And if the inclination toward pride is always near, how much more so when he hears that his deeds shall be praised in the gates, his enemy grows stronger and entices him with double persuasion to become proud. And he must be a man of war who overcomes his inclination at that time, in order to be saved from it, by thinking pure thoughts: what is the praise of creatures to me, or their honoring me? Since I know my own transgressions, and perhaps I am despised, abominable, filthy, and loathsome before my Creator and before the entire host on high — what does it give me and what does it add to me if people are mistaken about me? Woe is me over my brokenness, for my brokenness is as great as the sea before the scale and balances of justice that belong to the Lord, who judges every person according to what he is. Such and such things must the living take to heart, immediately when praised or honored, in order to be saved from pride — perhaps thereby.
Pele Yoetz 361:2: And since causing one's fellow to sin is worse than killing him, it is fitting to be exceedingly careful not to cause him to sin with the severe sin of pride, and not to praise him to his face, and not to tell him praise said of him not to his face, for there is much to be concerned about, lest, Heaven forbid, he sin and anger the blessed Creator with the severe sin of pride and his soul be lost, Heaven forbid. And even if he overcomes his inclination and does not sin, what business is it of yours to anger him with this contest? It is fitting to have regard for one's Maker's honor and for one's fellow's soul.
Pele Yoetz 361:3: And were it not that the Torah commanded honoring the wise, and our sages, of blessed memory, honored the wealthy (Eruvin 86a), I would also say that for this same reason it is fitting not to accord honor to anyone, since it injures the soul, as stated; and there is also the evil of honor itself, for it is written in Sefer Chasidim (section 8) that whatever benefit a person derives from the honor accorded him in this world is deducted, correspondingly, from his merits and his reward for the World to Come — and this applies even to one who deserves honor and is given it, how much more so to us, orphans of orphans, full of sins and deficiencies and lacking every good thing, that if we seek honor and pursue it and are resentful over it and grow proud through it — woe, what shall become of us? Behold, we have perished, we are lost, Heaven forbid. And who is the man who shall live and overcome his inclination so as not to benefit from honor and not become proud through it, for which reason it would seem that its absence would be better; but what shall we do, since our Father in Heaven has decreed upon us to honor everyone deserving of honor according to what our own physical eyes see — let the man being honored gather strength not to benefit from the honor and not become proud through it. But in any case I say that it is not fitting to praise and honor precious young men, trees still budding who have not been tested with honor, for upon seeing themselves praised or honored, it seems to them as though they were wise, learned, perfect in everything, with neither knowledge nor understanding like a beast, to lower themselves and recognize their limited worth and flee from honor; rather they climb their own heights and stand in the place of the great and clothe themselves in pride, and rule on halachic matters out of shame at not wanting to say they do not know, since it is a disgrace to them given the honor accorded them, and they think their name is like the name of the great, and they engage in dispute with the great and increase prosecution, and speak harshly and write harshly even to the holy ones who are in the land, from whose mouths we live and whose fingernail is thicker than our loins, and many other such evils, in such a way that it is fitting to call out regarding them (Song of Songs 2:15), “Catch us the little foxes that ruin the vineyards.” Who caused them all this? The honor accorded them and the praise given them to their face.
Pele Yoetz 361:4: And they already told in the Talmud (Bava Metzia 84b) that Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon used to sit on the ground before the sages and would raise difficulties, propose objections, and resolve them; they said, “We drink his water yet he sits on the ground” — they wished to honor him and raised him up and seated him on a bench. Rabbi Shimon said to them, “I have one mule and you wish to destroy it for me” (Rashi explained: through his becoming proud and through the evil eye). They reconsidered and lowered him again. Let the wise man hear and add learning, and let him seat his sons only among the knees of Torah scholars, and not let them speak words of Torah among common people who have not seen light, and a little that they see seems much in their eyes, and they increase praising and honoring them, and one must be concerned about all these mishaps and about the evil eye. And let him teach his sons and his students to be modest, as it is written (Proverbs 11:2), “And with the modest is wisdom,” and to recognize their limited worth and conduct themselves with truthfulness and righteous humility, so that they succeed in their studies.
Pele Yoetz 361:5: And even where they said (Eruvin 18b) that all of it is said not to his face, one must be careful that it not be in the presence of his enemies or in the presence of people who are not proper, who do not wish to hear people's praise, for they said (Arachin 16a): a person should not tell of his fellow's good, for from his good one comes to his disgrace — since the one telling or the one hearing says, “All his good traits he has, except this disgraceful one,” and it turns out they come to severe slander. And the masters of ethics already wrote, in this language: our sages said (Eruvin, ibid.) that they say part of his praise to his face and all of it not to his face, and woe to creatures who say praise that is not deserved to his face, and his disgrace not to his face, for flattery has grown strong. And a good man should tell of everyone's praise, for they told of one who saw a carcass and said, “How this carcass stinks,” and a pious man said to him, “See, its teeth are as white as pearls” — meaning that one should see and tell of someone's praise, not his disgrace. And through this a person is recognized, for a base person speaks basely, and whoever disqualifies others disqualifies through his own blemish, while a good man speaks good, and by the measure with which a person measures, he is measured from Heaven, whether for good or otherwise, and one who speaks good acquires advocates who speak good of him in the heavens above.
Pele Yoetz 362:1: Shogeg (Unwitting Sin) — A sin committed unwittingly requires repentance in full measure, and if he does not repent, he shall surely be punished, and “the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4). And at the time the Holy Temple stood, he would bring a sacrifice and repent and be atoned (see Yerushalmi Makkot 3:6), and even now repentance is required, and in place of a sacrifice, “let us render the words of our lips” [instead of bulls]. And the masses of the people think that when one sins unwittingly, he is entirely exempt, thinking, “What could I have done?” and even if he grieves a little, his grief soon passes — and this applies even to a deliberate sin. And a person grieves more over the loss of a single coin than he grieves over a single transgression, and this is because, through our many sins, our eyes have grown dark to seeing evil, for what harm we have caused above. And according to the truth, it is fitting to grieve and feel bitter over a transgression with anguish of soul, more and more than over the separation of his own soul from his body. And just as one who unwittingly kills his only son, his flesh pains him and his soul mourns over him, so, even more so, one should grieve over an unwitting transgression. And just as one who spills a jug of oil on his precious garments, even unwittingly, his garments become soiled, and if they are the king's garments, he shall be punished for not having opened his eyes and not having been exceedingly careful — and if it was under duress, though he shall not be punished, in any case he must rectify what he distorted and wash the garments well and repair them and restore them to their former state — so it is with this matter: the one who sins deliberately, his punishment grows greater for having let the willfulness of his heart carry him to anger the King to His face and rebel against His command and soil His sanctuary and His garments with the filth of his sins, and he blemishes Names and worlds and disrupts the channels of the flow, and many other evils the sinner causes. For all this he shall surely be punished with harsh and bitter sufferings. And if he wishes to be saved, he must mortify himself and accept sufferings upon himself as much as he can bear, and if sufferings come to him from Heaven, let him accept them with love and joy.
Pele Yoetz 362:2: And he must also rectify what he distorted, through confession, remorse, and abandonment of the sin, and endure further suffering to purify what he blemished and rectify what he distorted, in such a way that suffering is needed for two reasons: one, for having transgressed the word of the Merciful One; and one, to rectify what he distorted and wash away the filth of his sins and purify what he blemished and the like, and restore the matter to its former state. And if the sin was unwitting, it is true that he shall be punished for not having had fear of the Name before him to be exceedingly careful and stand guard to be saved from sin as from a sword, and for not having exerted himself to know the prohibition in order to separate from it; but his punishment shall not be as great as that of the deliberate sinner, though in any case he must rectify what he distorted just as the deliberate sinner must.
Pele Yoetz 362:3: And one must grieve additionally over an unwitting or compelled sin, for it is a sign and wonder that his soul is not pure, since the Holy One, blessed be He, does not bring about a mishap even through the animal of the righteous, how much more so through the righteous themselves (Yevamot 99b), and merit is brought about through the meritorious and guilt through the guilty, and the unwitting sinner shall eventually sin deliberately, for one transgression drags along another. And it is fitting for a person to pour out his soul before the Name, and let the Israelite man say: “If I am liable because of my sins, it is better that God, blessed be His Name, discipline me with harsh sufferings unto death, rather than that a mishap come about through my hand, and that guilt be brought about through me and I anger my Creator, Heaven forbid, for this is worse and more bitter to me than a thousand deaths.” And one who sins under compulsion, though he shall not be punished, since the Merciful One exempts one under compulsion, in any case he must rectify what he distorted and cleanse what he soiled, and this is why we say on Yom Kippur in the order “Al Chet,” “For the sin we sinned before You under compulsion” — for even the compelled sinner needs rectification through repentance, and he shall repent and be healed.
Pele Yoetz 363:1: Shoftim VeShotrim (Judges and Officers) is one of the 613 commandments: to appoint in every city and every province a judge who shall judge with righteousness, and officers who shall enforce the matter of judgment, for were it not for the fear of judges and officers, people would swallow each other alive, since they go to “our enemies as judges.” And besides that there is a great prohibition in the matter, for one who brings Israelite cases before gentiles desecrates the Name and glorifies idols by exalting them, as it is said (Deuteronomy 32:31), “For their rock is not like our Rock, and our enemies are themselves judges” — when our enemies are the judges, this is testimony to the exaltation of their fear, so said our sages, of blessed memory, and Rashi, of blessed memory, brought it at the beginning of Parashat Mishpatim. And there is a further grievous evil, that all their judgments are crooked and perverse, and their intention leans toward whoever gives more in the case, and it turns out that robbery increases and the land is filled with violence. Therefore an obligation rests upon one to appoint a judge, and even if there is no sage in the city, three God-fearing laypeople shall be appointed, and by their word shall be settled every matter of judgment between a person and his fellow, and they shall not allow the children of Israel to go to litigate in gentile courts. And if some worthless man goes out of line and takes his fellow to gentile courts, they shall strike him and write against him and pursue him to utter destruction, as our master ruled in the Shulchan Aruch, Choshen Mishpat, section 388. And woe to a generation in whose days this has come to pass, that there are great cities in the cities of Edom that have tens of thousands of Israelites, and Torah has been forgotten among them, and they judge only in gentile courts, and this has become treated as permitted by them — may the Good Name grant them atonement.
Pele Yoetz 363:2: And its ruling is that, through our many sins, we have no officers to enforce the law and we must make use of gentiles, our judicial enemies, to compel [judgment], and we cannot fulfill the commandment of appointing officers except through the leaders of the community, and those who have influence and standing and closeness with the authorities and with the judges, who shall stand at the judge's right hand to raise up the banner of the Torah, and whoever does not heed the judge's voice shall be compelled through bans and excommunications or through gentiles. And I praise the custom of our Ashkenazic brothers, who strike and beat with sticks and imprison, by the hand of Israel, whoever goes out of line or does not fulfill Torah law, and do not hand over an Israelite's body or his money into the hand of gentiles — happy are they, how good is their portion. And I have already written on this matter above under the entry Mishpat VeDin — see there.
Pele Yoetz 364:1: Shochet (Ritual Slaughterer) — The slaughterers can say, “We bring our bread at the risk of our lives” (Lamentations 5:9), for in every trade one must be careful that a man not transgress and go out of line for the sake of a piece of bread, but the slaughterers' work is heavy, since they must detect the tiniest, subtlest nick, and need a clear and settled mind, for many times a person passes his fingernail over the knife two or three times and finds no nick, and on the fourth he finds it, and it recurs and reappears, and he must have exceeding fear of Heaven to be exceedingly precise in examining the knife and examining the lungs, and let the man tremble and shrink from feeding non-kosher meat to Israel, for whoever does this bears the sin of the many and his sin is greater than can be borne, and he deserves to be thrown to the dogs, since he has taken what belongs to them and fed it to Israel. And it is fitting for every slaughterer to show his knife, from time to time, to every sage and every slaughterer, and he should be concerned lest he has lost his sensitivity, since it is a routine, ongoing matter, and two are better than one. And an obligation rests upon him to go over the laws at least twice a year, until they are fluent in his mouth and he is expert in them. And if some doubt arises for him, if there is a sage or another slaughterer in the city, he should not rely on his own knowledge to permit or forbid, but rather he must ask. And they already said in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 7b) that when a case of non-kosher meat came before Rava, he would gather all the butchers together, saying, “So that a beam's weight of guilt should reach them” [i.e., so that the responsibility be shared]. And what shall we, orphans of orphans, say after this?
Pele Yoetz 364:2: And if he wishes to be stringent and forbid what is permitted, if it is an Israelite's money, there is a prohibition in that he causes an Israelite's money to be lost, and if it is a gentile's money, this too is not good, for through our sins many animals contain reincarnated souls, and one must be concerned lest that animal contains some reincarnated soul that deserved to be rectified, and if he declares it non-kosher unnecessarily, it turns out he injures a soul. And there is already a story told of Rabbi Yisrael Baal Shem Tov, who went to a certain house and saw a piece of meat hanging on a nail, and asked that they cook some of it for him; they told him it was non-kosher meat set aside for the gentile of the house. He said, “How can this be, for it requested and pleaded with me to eat from it?” They immediately called the slaughterer, and he inquired and investigated and found that he had erred in the ruling, and he [the Baal Shem Tov] ate from it in order to rectify the soul that was in it. For this let the slaughterer and the judge tremble and shrink from declaring what is permitted as forbidden, and let the slaughterer have this intention in his slaughtering and in his blessing over the slaughter.
Pele Yoetz 364:3: And let the slaughterer be exceedingly careful with the commandment of covering the blood and its blessing, and regarding this too I shall tell the generation what I saw: a certain slaughterer whose eyes became afflicted with a lengthy illness, until he took to his bed and died. And he came in a dream to a certain girl from the city, saying that this slaughterer had once slaughtered a fowl and did not cover its blood, and in that fowl's blood a certain Israelite man's soul was reincarnated, ready to be rectified through the commandment of covering; and since he did not cover the blood, the soul remained wandering and found no rest, and because of this sin this illness came upon his eyes. I have told this story today because there are many slaughterers in our time to whom commandments are not dear, and who are lenient regarding the commandment of covering the blood — let them hear this and let the hair of their heads stand on end. And let the slaughterer tremble when coming to slaughter, considering this, for sometimes the slaughterer of the ox strikes a man. And how good it is for the slaughterer to precede his work with prayer that no mishap result from his hand and that he merit to rectify the souls that are reincarnated. And it is already found in the book Shevet Musar, chapter 1, which speaks of the slaughterers, and there is stated a text of prayer for the slaughterers — see there.
Pele Yoetz 364:4: And how greatly must the slaughterer fence himself in so as not to err in his judgment when examining the knife, and not examine it while drunk, nor while drowsy with sleep, nor while he has a cold, nor in a place of confusion and shouting, nor hastily, nor while tired, for the examination requires a clear mind, like a clear day.
Pele Yoetz 364:5: And I have seen God-fearing slaughterers who were careful not to examine the knife after examining the lungs, since then the fingernail is soft and cannot examine well. And given the great care required and the limited settlement and preparation found in some cities, I say that eating meat is a tremendous danger, and it is a great evil if one stumbles into eating forbidden food, for the body is built up on forbidden food and his body becomes a piece of the forbidden, and how can he attain the paths of life — “Depart, unclean,” they shall call to them. And happy is he who can withstand and be careful not to eat meat at all, or at least not to eat anything but poultry, which he can be careful to slaughter with a settled mind — how good is his portion and how pleasant is his lot, especially in this orphaned generation when slaughterers have multiplied in the villages who have no fear of the Name before them and have neither knowledge nor understanding to know the laws thoroughly, and do not know how to touch books, having learned only a little law orally. And the blame hangs on the necks of the slaughterers and the rabbis who grant them ordination certificates without examining well and thoroughly whether they are expert and whether fear of sin preceded them. It is good for a man who travels the road and fears the Name, if he cannot examine the slaughterer and is not certain of him, to withdraw his hand and not eat from his slaughtering, for stumbling is common among such slaughterers. And the early and later authorities have already cried out about this, and there is no remedy until the world is rectified under the kingdom of the Almighty. In any case, whoever wishes to be concerned for himself and be careful should conduct his affairs discreetly and not reveal it, either because of arrogance or so as not to increase disputes in Israel, and this is a great principle in all matters of piety: the reward for all is modesty.
Pele Yoetz 365:1: Shammash (Servant/Attendant) — A servant who attends either an individual or the public must be trustworthy to his employers, diligent, swift in his work, performing the work properly, and let his employer's money be as dear to him as his own, and let him strive to discern his employer's mind to do their will as their will without being told. And when they tell him something, let him free himself from all his other affairs immediately and do what he was told swiftly, in such a way that they need not tell him a second time. And let him be trustworthy to the utmost degree, not benefiting from even a small coin of theirs without their permission. And not only should he heed and do his master's will, but he should also heed his master's wife and all the members of his household and do their will. And he should also heed his master's relatives, and let all the members of his master's household be dear to him, and let him show them extraordinary affection as though they were members of his own household. And likewise a synagogue attendant should serve all the members of the synagogue equally, rich and poor, young and old, and not turn so much toward monetary gain, but rather do what is incumbent upon him with wholehearted sincerity, and find favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and in the eyes of his employers, and honor shall come in the end.
Pele Yoetz 365:2: And if his employers curse and revile him, let him bow his head and lower his eyes, and not respond even if it seems to him that he is in the right and they revile him for no reason out of their harshness, or because of their anger and bitterness of spirit over some other matter; rather let him bear it and accept everything with love as atonement for his sins, until Heaven looks favorably and has mercy on him. And let him not reveal his employers' secrets and not tell of their affairs, and not speak of their disgrace even with the members of his own household, and let him accept Heaven's judgment with love, that His wisdom, blessed be His Name, has decreed that there be servants and masters in the world, and thereby he shall fulfill what is written in the Torah (Leviticus 19:18), “And you shall love your neighbor as yourself” — for just as he would want to be served diligently, cleanly, with wholehearted sincerity, a complete and whole service, so let him serve his employers, and let him reason on that day, an a fortiori argument for himself: if he serves flesh and blood like himself in this manner for the sake of monetary gain given to him grudgingly, how much more so must he serve his Creator and Maker, from whose hand comes everything he has from the day of his birth until the day of his death, and who repays good reward to those who do His will. And so let him not neglect his Creator's service, such as the Shema, prayers, and blessings, and let him not transgress the words of the Torah or the words of the Sages for the sake of serving flesh and blood. And let him stipulate with his employers that he not bring his bread at the risk of his soul, for it is better for a person to die of hunger than to be wicked before the Omnipresent for even one hour; rather, let him hold to this and also to that, for everything has its time, and there is a time for every purpose, for one who is diligent and swift in his work, and let fear of the Name always be before him. If he does thus, then he shall prosper in his ways and then he shall have understanding, and servants shall become masters, and a free servant more than his own master, either in this world or the World to Come. These are some aspects of the paths of servants, whether serving an individual or the public, whether a son serving his father or a wife her husband; let the wise man hear and add learning, to be like servants who serve their master not in order to receive a reward, but out of love, with affection, with a cheerful countenance and a pleasant expression.
Pele Yoetz 365:3: And whoever is a synagogue attendant should also intend, in his work, work of Heaven for the sake of a commandment, and honor the synagogue and grant merit to the many by calling them to the synagogue every day for the morning, afternoon, and evening prayers. And if he merits that someone rises for his sake and comes to the synagogue to pray, his reward is greater than all the payment he receives from the congregation. And likewise let his eyes be open toward wandering guests, to arrange for them sufficient food for their needs, by collecting from the people of the city day by day and Shabbat by Shabbat, a matter in its proper time, and appease them with good words and a cheerful countenance — it shall be counted as a great commandment for him and he shall bear a blessing from the Name. Not so if he does not arrange sufficient food for their needs at the proper time, or scolds them in the manner of some coarse attendants — his sin is greater than can be borne, for he sins against one who is not his own to sin against, and if the poor person cries out, the Name shall hear his outcry and curse the attendant's portion, Heaven forbid.
Pele Yoetz 365:4: And it is known what we have established, that one engaged in communal needs is considered as one engaged in Torah (Yerushalmi Berachot 5:1). Behold, therefore, let the attendant be diligent in performing communal needs with all his heart for the sake of a commandment. And whoever serves, even an individual, should have this as second nature, and then accustom himself until it becomes second nature to him to be among the insulted who do not insult, hearing their disgrace and not responding, and not being resentful about anything in the world. And especially one who serves the public cannot fulfill his obligation to everyone, for this one says thus and that one says thus, this one holds one view and that one holds another, and he must bear it all. And not only if something imperfect comes from his own hand, requiring him to accept and hear rebuke, but even if another did something improper and wishes to vent his anger on this man, he must bear this too and hear the rebuke, and through this he shall increase peace and find favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man.
Pele Yoetz 365:5: And it is known, the statement of our sages, of blessed memory, who said (Berachot 7b): greater is attending [on sages] than studying [under them]. And great is the kindness a person performs with his body more than with his money. Behold, therefore, the man who does not have the strength to benefit a Torah scholar with his possessions, or even if he has the strength and benefits him with a fine portion, let him do all that is in his power to do and serve Torah scholars with all his strength, arranging their food and all their needs so that they be free to engage in Torah, and through this the Name shall account it to him as though he himself were engaged in Torah, and he takes the foremost portion in what the sage studies, besides that the Holy One, blessed be He, establishes reward for him for honoring the Torah and its students, and he eats the fruits in this world while the principal remains for the World to Come, provided he serve them with heart and soul like a person doing his own work, with diligence and affection. And let him strive to acquire everything good and cheap for them, and if the Name widens his boundary, when he buys expensively, let him sell to them cheaply so that it be pleasant to them and they eat with joy to warm themselves, and it shall be counted as charity for him. And this is the commandment of a son toward his father and a wife toward her husband, to serve them — this is their honor. Therefore let not the burden of the work be heavy upon them, since they reckon the reward of the commandment and that they give satisfaction to their Maker.
Pele Yoetz 365:6: And employers must have compassion on their workers and not work them harshly but with gentle speech, and not be angry with them, revile them, or curse them, for it is enough that he has merited to be an employer, and it is their trouble's own judgment that they are servants of servants. And even if they do something improper, let him guide and lead them with gentle speech, and let him not starve them and not overwork them excessively, and not wake them in the middle of their sleep, and let him have compassion on them as a father has compassion on his children, for we are all children of one man, children of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And it is written (Deuteronomy 15:16), “And it is good for him with you.” Our sages, of blessed memory, said (Kiddushin 15a): “with you” in food, “with you” in drink. And though the verse speaks of a slave, we learn from it also regarding a hired worker, for this is the straight path. And at least let him give him to taste from everything he eats and fulfill in him, “And you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” And by the measure with which a person measures and conducts himself with his servant, his wife, and the members of his household who are under his authority, so is he measured from Heaven. And let him reckon that far more than what they owe him, he owes his Creator, and through this he shall remove his anger and conduct himself toward them with the attribute of kindness and the attribute of mercy, so that mercy be shown to him from Heaven. And there are people who, for this reason, choose to employ gentiles, so that they can rule over them harshly, but this is not the straight path, for it is better for a person to toil greatly so that Israelites be supported from his possessions, even if the members of his own household are poor, and it shall be counted as charity for him when he gives his money to one who gives satisfaction to his Creator through it, rather than to one who angers our Creator through it, since it is possible he shall go and buy an offering for idolatry with it. And it is already written in the books that because of this sin, householders decline in their possessions and their wealth is lost through evil circumstances, and their offspring seek bread, and let him not be gracious to orphans, just as he had no compassion on the poor to bring them close to benefit. Therefore, where there is an Israelite who can serve him, a person should not give his money to a gentile, and when he gives to the Israelite who serves him, let him give with a generous eye so that his soul bless him, and this is the essence of charity in secret, as I have written elsewhere.
Pele Yoetz 365:7: And behold, just as it is forbidden to strike one's grown son lest one cause him to stumble into disrespecting him (Mo'ed Katan 17a), so a father regarding sons whom he knows to be rebellious and defiant, not heeding their father's and mother's voice, should refrain from commanding them to do something, since it turns out he causes them to stumble and brings it about that they commit a blemish and cause grief and anger above and be punished on his account — therefore its absence is better, and it all depends on how he recognizes his sons' nature and traits. Happy is the man who is diligent and serves himself and does not ask others to serve him — this man is diligent and rewarded and shall live a life of tranquility and be saved from anger and shall increase peace. But if he sees that they are God-fearing, that they desire the commandment, he too should intend for their merit.
Pele Yoetz 366:1: Sechar Sachir (A Worker's Wage) — Paying a hired worker's wage on the day it is due is one of the 613 commandments, as it is written (Deuteronomy 24:15), “On his day you shall give him his wage.” And the kabbalists wrote that the segulah of this commandment, when fulfilled during the days of the week, is that one merits, on that Shabbat, an additional soul, spirit, and higher soul. And given this great benefit, it is fitting for whoever the Name has graced with means to seek to give out work during the week in order to fulfill this commandment, and how much more so, an obligation rests upon the members of the community to pay the wages of all those who work for the public — such as cantors, attendants, and teachers — on their due day, week by week. And it is a bad practice done in some villages, where they give a list to the community's servants that they collect from individuals, and there are several individuals who do not pay on time and put off the servants from day to day, saying “come back,” and they cry out and are not answered — this is certainly the sin of the community and a disgrace to them, that the many should be indebted to the individual and not pay on the due day those who work for the public in the work of Heaven, so that they wander for bread — let there be no such thing in Israel.
Pele Yoetz 367:1: Sechar Mitzvah (The Reward of a Commandment) — We have learned there (Avot 2:1): reckon the reward of a commandment. This is a great principle for all of Judaism, for a person toils one day to earn ten lira or even less, and for the prospect of a hundred lira he would agree to toil a week, and if the prospect were a thousand lira he would agree to toil a month, and if the prospect were a thousand gold coins he would agree to toil a year or several years amid every toil in the world, ascending mountains and descending valleys, going down to the sea in ships, in the heat by day and the frost by night, and many other evils that pass over the souls of merchants who eat the bread of sorrow — and all this is as nothing compared to the benefit of the prospect he thinks to earn, perhaps he shall earn it. And sometimes, after all the toil and effort, he loses and does not earn, and returns to toil again to see if perhaps he shall earn. And even if he earns abundant spoil, it is all vanity and vexation of spirit, and what advantage has a person in all his toil, even if his hand has attained much, for he shall not take it all with him at his death, but only what he sends before him: commandments and good deeds. And if you ask anyone called by the name of Israel how much Torah and good deeds are worth, he shall answer that no silver or gold in the world could match its value, and no desirable things compare to it. And this is true and firmly established: that whoever performs any commandment whatsoever, whether in thought, speech, or deed, certainly and without any doubt earns far greater profit than one who finds abundant spoil. And whoever transgresses a single transgression, whether he transgresses a positive commandment or a negative commandment, his loss is far greater than one who loses immense wealth and greater than one who loses his life — this is a truth clear as the sun, all Israel believes this. It follows that whoever transgresses any commandment, or commits any transgression with contempt of soul, is comparable to one who takes a purse of gold coins and throws it into the sea, or comparable to one who destroys himself knowingly. And our sages, of blessed memory, said well (Sotah 3a): a person does not sin unless a spirit of folly has entered him, for there is no greater fool than this. Such things let the living take to heart, and let him run like a deer and gather strength like a lion to fulfill every good thing and flee from every hint of prohibition, and regarding this it is said (Proverbs 2:4-5), “If you seek it as silver and search for it as for hidden treasures, then you shall understand the fear of the Lord.”
Pele Yoetz 367:2: And behold, this is a ladder set upon the earth to ascend the mountain of the Lord and stand in His holy place, for out of doing it not for its own sake one comes to do it for its own sake, since in his heart he shall understand that it is fitting to serve the Name not in order to receive a reward, but rather to give Him satisfaction specifically, for there is no greater reward in the world than this: that a great King, exalted and lofty, awesome and fearsome, is pleased with a person, mere breath that he is, that he serve before Him and that his deeds be acceptable and give satisfaction before His glorious throne. And how precious and great an attainment it is for a man whom a king of flesh and blood desires and raises from the dust to stand and serve before him, and who finds satisfaction from serving him and delights in him — how much more so, greater beyond measure and without limit, is the good that comes to us in that the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, desires us and receives satisfaction from our deeds and builds worlds through our good deeds; were there no reward but this, it would be enough for us and sufficient. And would that, if we are deserving of some good reward in this world and the World to Come, He should repay us with this: that we give further satisfaction to our Creator, for this is the good reward. Know this, for they said (Avot 4:17): one hour of tranquility of spirit in the World to Come is better than all the life of this world. And nevertheless they said (ibid.): one hour of Torah and good deeds in this world is better than all the life of the World to Come. Happy is the man who has found wisdom and attained this trait — this is the whole of man.
Pele Yoetz 368:1: Sechel (Understanding) — A man is praised according to his understanding, that he have good understanding so that he walk in the way of the good and keep the paths of the righteous (Proverbs 2:20), and conduct himself with good traits and uprightness in the eyes of God and man, and know how to conduct himself with every person according to his traits, and do every good thing and distance himself from every evil thing. Understanding shall be king over all the internal and external limbs, and it shall rule over them to guide and lead them in the straight path, so that they abandon their bad habit of doing improper deeds and bad traits, and whatever straight understanding desires, so shall be done — it shall not rebel against its word, and the inclination shall not rule over the understanding, and one shall not acquire a master for oneself. And whoever lacks understanding, his evil is great, for “the way of a fool is upright in his own eyes”; but in any case let him go to the wise and roll in the dust of their feet and drink their words with thirst, and study or hear teachings — perhaps there is hope that he shall acquire good understanding. And they already said (Vayikra Rabbah 1:6; Yalkut Shimoni, Proverbs, remez 959): if you have acquired knowledge, what do you lack? And if you lack knowledge, what have you acquired? And understanding is good for all who possess it and conduct themselves according to straight understanding — not so one who does not act according to the understanding and wisdom the Name has graced him with; “adding knowledge adds pain” (Ecclesiastes 1:18), for unwitting errors become like deliberate acts, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Pesikta Zuta, Nitzavim 29:18). And in this let the wise man glory in his wisdom — understanding and knowing (Jeremiah 9:23) the Name and doing what is good and upright.
Pele Yoetz 369:1: Shem Tov (A Good Name) — We have learned (Avot 4:13): there are three crowns — the crown of Torah, the crown of priesthood, and the crown of kingship — but the crown of a good name surpasses them all. That is, that his deeds and the perfection of his traits shall be praised in the gates. And there is no need for him to publicize his deeds or praise himself, for it is written (Proverbs 27:2), “Let a stranger praise you, and not your own mouth”; rather, let him do his deeds in secret specifically for the sake of Heaven, and honor shall come in the end, even though he does his own part, as it is indeed fitting to conceal one's deeds to the utmost degree and flee from honor — honor shall come in the end and pursue him, and the Holy One, blessed be He, publicizes his deeds, for it is written (Jeremiah 23:24), “Can a man hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him?” and our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Yalkut Shimoni, Jeremiah, remez 305): I shall show him to others. And whatever a person does in secret, whether good or bad, the Holy One, blessed be He, brings it to light, and he acquires a good name or a bad name, and the children of Israel, even if they are not prophets, are the children of prophets and recognize every person and regard him according to what he is. And a person is recognized by his purse, his cup, his anger, his words, and his movements, and to every sight of a person's eyes, whether his deed is pure and upright or whether his inside matches his outside, or whether he is among the hypocrites — understanding is easy for the discerning, and even if he can deceive people for a time, appearing to the eyes as one thing, in the end his disgrace shall be revealed, and nothing remains hidden forever in this world.
Pele Yoetz 369:2: And behold, in the holy Zohar it is told of a certain man named Elazar who became a complete penitent, and they said of him that perhaps the reason was that God helped him [a wordplay on his name, “God has helped”]. And in the Midrash they said (Bereishit Rabbah 37:7; see Yalkut Shimoni, Noach, remez 62) that the righteous name their sons after the event, in remembrance of the kindnesses of the blessed God. Behold, therefore, it is good for a man to give a good name to his sons, and not insist on naming them after their forebears, for what does it give or add? Go and learn from the early generations, who did not use their forebears' names, and if the name causes them a little assistance to walk in the way of the good, is this not a better name than seven names of their forebears? Therefore a good man should choose to give his sons a good name, or a name after the event, to recall the kindnesses of the Name, and he should utter this with his lips at the time of naming. And it is found written in the books that for one whose children do not survive, let him name his son Ben Zion, or give him two names, and he shall live with the help of the blessed Name.
Pele Yoetz 370:1: Shiur (Measure) — There are things that have no fixed measure, and this is a great principle in all traits: a perfect medium, as we have learned (Avot 2:1): which is the straight path that a person should choose for himself? Whatever is glorious to the one who does it and glorious to him among men — that he not turn to either of the two extremes. And this is a matter that cannot all be explained in writing, for not every person, not every time, not every place, and not every matter are alike, and a person must be wise and understand from his own knowledge, and weigh with a scale and balances of justice which is the straight path to conduct himself, according to what kind of person he is in the eyes of others, and according to what kind of people they are according to their traits, and according to the place and according to the time — so shall he conduct himself according to the need of the hour, neither too long nor too short, neither too much nor too little. And for this one needs correct understanding and mercy, to ask the Name regarding this secret, that He rectify him with good counsel to do what is good and upright, a matter in its proper time, in a manner that finds favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man.
Pele Yoetz 370:2: And all the measures that the sages fixed must be carefully observed, such as an olive's volume of matzah and an olive's volume of maror on the night of Passover, and drinking the four cups, and the cup of Kiddush and the cup of Grace after Meals, and the cup of Havdalah and the like, which require the measure of a revi'it, and less than an olive's volume does not suffice, that is, nine dirhams, because of the doubt regarding the concluding blessing, for some say the concluding blessing must be recited over an olive's volume, and some say a revi'it, that is, twenty-six dirhams, is required. Therefore, to satisfy the doubt where a concluding blessing is required, one must drink a full revi'it. And both man and woman are equal in their measures. And many err and are not precise about the measures, and their evil is great, for if they are not precise about eating an olive's volume of matzah and an olive's volume of maror, it turns out that their blessing over eating matzah and over eating maror is in vain, and they neglect the commandment. And likewise, if they are not precise about drinking the four cups and Kiddush and Havdalah and Grace after Meals, they do not fulfill the commandment, and it turns out they eat without Kiddush and without Havdalah, and if they recite the concluding blessing, it is a blessing in vain, since it requires a measure. These are some of the evils of the common people, transgressing the commandments even unwittingly — may the Good Name grant atonement, and “he who walks with the wise shall become wise” (Proverbs 13:20).
Pele Yoetz 371:1: Shesh (Linen) — The kabbalists wrote of the segulah of dressing a deceased person in linen garments, that it protects from all evil spirits and all prosecutions, and his flesh shall dwell securely. Behold, therefore, it is fitting for a person to have regard for himself and his deceased, and command regarding himself that his shrouds be made of linen garments without any admixture of other material at all. And in a place where it is customary to include cotton wool, let them include flax fibers instead, and let the tallit too be of flax with flax threads.
Pele Yoetz 371:2: And it is good for a man to prepare his own shrouds while he is still in his prime, and make them as he wishes, and have them ready for him, for a person does not know his time or his place — it is possible his death might occur on Friday afternoon after midday, or on the eve of a festival, or on some day close to darkness, and since the shrouds are not ready, they would need to let him lie overnight, which is a great blemish and grief for the soul; but with the shrouds ready, they can hasten his burial. Or perhaps his death might occur on the road, and there his burial would be without shrouds — therefore it is good that they be ready for him, and wherever he goes, let him take them with him, and through this the day of death shall always be remembered by him, and he shall walk in the way of the good.
